extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent applicants, agents, and attorneys
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for establishing/commonality of ownership or invoking a joint research agreement to disqualify pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e),(f),(g) references under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) (including CREATE Act/JRA procedures) and related examiner procedures (including provisional rejections and double patenting treatment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Common ownership requirement under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common ownership (or an obligation to assign) of the subject matter and the claimed invention must exist at the time the claimed invention was made for the subject matter to be disqualified as prior art under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c). Actual ownership or a legal obligation to assign both the subject matter and the claimed invention to the same individual(s) or organization(s)/business entity(ies) must be in existence at the time the claimed invention was made; a moral or unenforceable obligation does not suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that principal ownership rights in different persons/organizations means common ownership does not exist; a license where basic ownership rights are retained does not defeat ownership; requirement is intended to preclude obtaining ownership after the invention date to disqualify prior art. Includes illustrative examples (parent-subsidiary, percentage ownership scenarios, joint ventures) showing when common ownership exists or does not exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof to establish disqualification under 103(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of establishing that subject matter is disqualified as prior art under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) rests upon the person(s) urging disqualification (e.g., the applicant or patentee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant or patentee must present evidence of common ownership at the time the claimed invention was made; placing the burden on the examiner or a litigation defendant is not appropriate because evidence of common ownership may be unavailable to them but should be readily available to the applicant/patentee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of applicant’s signed statement to establish common ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications and references will be considered owned by, or subject to an obligation of assignment to, the same person at the time the invention was made if the applicant(s) or patent owner(s) make a signed statement to that effect (signed in accordance with 37 CFR 1.33(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statement should be clear and conspicuous (e.g., on a separate piece of paper). Such a signed statement alone is sufficient to disqualify a reference (example language provided). Applicants/owners may, but are not required to, submit additional evidence (assignments, affidavits/declarations, court decisions). See USPTO guideline citation: “Guidelines Setting Forth a Modified Policy Concerning the Evidence of Common Ownership...” (1241 OG 96).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective evidence categories to establish common ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: If further evidence is submitted or required, acceptable objective evidence includes recorded assignments, unrecorded assignments filed in each application, an affidavit or declaration by the common owner, or other evidence establishing common ownership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details: (A) reference to assignments recorded in the USPTO (37 CFR Part 3) conveying entire rights to the same person(s)/organization(s); (B) copies of unrecorded assignments filed in the applications; (C) affidavit/declaration by an empowered official of the corporation/organization explaining and stating facts supporting common ownership and properly signed; (D) any other evidence submitted in the application or patent that establishes common ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner action when independent evidence raises material doubt
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner has independent evidence that raises a material doubt as to the accuracy of an applicant’s representation of common ownership or the existence of an obligation to assign, the examiner may explain the doubt and require objective evidence of common ownership or obligation to assign as of the date of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should explain why the accuracy of the representation is doubted. Note that execution dates in assignment documents may not reflect the date a party was under an obligation to assign; examiner may require evidence such as assignments or declarations. This is an exception to treating the applicant’s signed statement as sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint research agreement (JRA) definition and timing for CREATE Act disqualification
rubrics_metrics.description: A joint research agreement for purposes of pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(3) is a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement entered into by two or more persons or entities for performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention that was in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The JRA must be shown to be in effect on or before the time the later invention was made; it need not be in effect on or before the prior art date of the reference to be disqualified. The JRA may be in effect prior to the CREATE Act effective date. Examples show JRAs that are effective (or not) for disqualification depending on timing and scope of activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements to invoke CREATE Act / JRA‑based disqualification
rubrics_metrics.description: To invoke disqualification under the CREATE Act (pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) as amended), the applicant/patent owner must provide a statement that the subject matter and the claimed invention were made by or on behalf of the parties to a JRA (within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. 100(h) and § 1.9(e)), that the JRA was in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made, and that the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the JRA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additionally, the application must disclose or be amended to disclose the names of the parties to the JRA. The statement should be on or begin on a separate sheet, must not address other matters (37 CFR 1.4(c)), and must be signed per 37 CFR 1.33(b). Applicants may submit supporting evidence but are not required to do so. See 37 CFR 1.71(g) and 1.104(c)(4) for form and processing requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing, fees, and correction rules for 37 CFR 1.71(g) JRA amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment under 37 CFR 1.71(g) to disclose the names of the parties to a JRA must be accompanied by the processing fee set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(i) if not filed within specified time periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specified time periods: (i) within three months of the filing date of a national application; (ii) within three months of entry of the national stage under 37 CFR 1.491; (iii) before mailing of a first Office action on the merits; or (iv) before mailing of a first Office action after filing an RCE under 37 CFR 1.114. If filed after the issue fee is paid, the issued patent may not include the names and must be corrected by certificate of correction under 35 U.S.C. 255 and 37 CFR 1.323 for the amendment to be effective. Reissue or reexamination is unnecessary solely to add names of parties to a JRA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination procedure when common ownership or JRA has not been established
rubrics_metrics.description: If the application file has not established that the reference is disqualified under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c), the examiner will assume the reference is not disqualified and examine on all grounds other than any conflict arising from a possible 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection based on pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e),(f) and/or (g).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should: (A) assume reference not disqualified; (B) examine application on all grounds other than conflicts arising from possible 103 rejections based on pre‑AIA 102(e)/(f)/(g); (C) consider applicability of references under 35 U.S.C. 103 based on such prior art, including provisional rejections under MPEP § 2146.03(a); and (D) apply best references under 102 and 103 until such time the reference is disqualified. If a statement of common ownership or assignment is filed in reply to a 103 rejection and claims are not amended, the examiner may not make the next Office action final if a new rejection is made (MPEP § 706.07(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination procedure when common ownership or JRA has been established
rubrics_metrics.description: If the application has established that the reference is disqualified under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c), the examiner will examine the application as to all grounds except pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e),(f) and (g) (as they apply through 35 U.S.C. 103), and will examine for double patenting and invite terminal disclaimers when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically: (A) examine all grounds except pre‑AIA 102(e)/(f)/(g) as they apply through 35 U.S.C. 103; (B) examine for statutory and nonstatutory double patenting and make a provisional rejection if appropriate; (C) invite applicant to file a terminal disclaimer under 37 CFR 1.321 to overcome provisional/actual nonstatutory double patenting rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double patenting treatment where disqualification applies
rubrics_metrics.description: A disqualified reference (treated as commonly owned under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) as amended by CREATE) may give rise to double patenting rejections between applications not owned by the same party; such disqualified subject matter will be treated as if commonly owned for double patenting analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double patenting rejections can be overcome in appropriate circumstances by filing a terminal disclaimer under 37 CFR 1.321 (including a provision that the later patent is enforceable only while commonly owned with the application/patent forming the basis for the rejection). The practice prevents improperly extended patent protection and is authorized by case law (e.g., In re Bowers). See MPEP §§ 804, 804.02, and 1490, subsection VI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional rejection (obviousness) using provisional prior art under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e)
rubrics_metrics.description: When two copending applications of different inventive entities are unpublished under 35 U.S.C. 122(b) and have differing filing dates, a provisional rejection under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) based on provisional prior art under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) should be made in the later‑filed application unless the application has been excluded under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: to alert the applicant that an actual rejection on the same ground may issue if one application issues, and to preserve confidentiality. Provisional rejections of obviousness type can be applied to copending applications having different effective filing dates with common assignee or common inventor. Ways to overcome include: (A) arguing patentability over the earlier filed application; (B) combining subject matter into a single application claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 and abandoning copending applications (with caution re: 35 U.S.C. 112/enablement/priority); (C) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing derivation (not invention “by another”); (D) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(a) showing an earlier date of invention prior to the effective U.S. filing date of the copending application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrative examples of ownership and JRA scenarios
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples illustrate application of the common ownership and JRA rules (e.g., parent company owning 100% of subsidiaries -> common ownership; parent owning 100% and 90% -> not common; joint venture ownership and obligations to assign result in common ownership; timing/scope of JRA determines eligibility for CREATE Act protection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples 1–8 for common ownership and multiple examples for JRA illustrate fact‑specific determinations: requirement that common ownership/JRA exist at the time the later invention was made; examples showing when a later-formed JRA or JRA limited to different activities does not qualify; example showing that wholly owned subsidiary transfers preserve common ownership.
